steps: The name is written as the Sumerogram EN.LÍL (𒂗𒆤), literally 'lord of the wind/air'.
The divine determinative 𒀭 (dingir) marks the name as a deity; it is silent in pronunciation.
In Akkadian scholarly tradition the long vowel is marked with a macron: Enlīl.
Enlīl was the chief god of the Sumerian pantheon, dwelling in the Ekur temple at Nippur.
provenance.etymology: Sumerian EN 'lord' + LÍL 'wind, air, spirit'; hence 'Lord of the Air/Wind'.
provenance.semantics: Chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon, god of air, storms, and destiny.
uncertainties: The exact vocalisation of Sumerian words is reconstructed; the macron on ī is a convention of modern scholarship.
The semantic range of LÍL includes 'wind', 'air', and 'ghost', making the precise nuance of the name debated.
provenance.dnsNotes: The Unicode restoration Enlīl uses a macron to preserve length; the ASCII form Enlil loses the vowel-length marker. The cuneiform form is not registrable in .com.

zeus.timePeriod: Ancient Greek, c. 8th century BCE – present

signs.name: zēta
signs.note: In Attic, Ζ represents the voiced affricate [zd], a retention of PIE *dy- in the name *dyēws.

signs.name: epsilon
signs.note: Short front vowel; here part of the diphthong ευ.

signs.name: upsilon
signs.note: In the diphthong ευ it is pronounced [u]; the diphthong counts as long for accent.

signs.name: sigma (final)
signs.note: Final sigma; nominative singular ending of the archaic stem *dyēu-s.

steps: The Greek form Ζεύς is attested from Mycenaean di-we / Diwos and Homeric Greek.
The initial Ζ- in Attic represents the voiced affricate [zd], preserving the PIE cluster *dy- from *dyēws 'sky, god of the sky'.
The diphthong ευ is long for accentual purposes and carries the acute accent, producing the single pitch peak Zeús.
The final -ς is the nominative singular ending of the archaic stem *dyēu-s.
provenance.etymology: From Proto-Indo-European *dyēws 'sky, daylight, sky-god'. Cognates: Sanskrit Dyáuṣ Pitā, Latin Juppiter (*dyēws ph₂tḗr), Germanic *Tīwaz (English Tuesday).
provenance.semantics: King of the Olympian gods; god of the sky, thunder, law, kingship, and cosmic order.

attestations.text: ἀλλ᾽, ὦ Ζεῦ καὶ Γῆ καὶ Ἐρινύες...

uncertainties: The exact phonetic value of initial Ζ in Archaic/Classical Attic is debated (affricate [zd] vs. fricative [z]).
The original nominative stem may have been *Diw- with ablaut variants.
provenance.dnsNotes: The Unicode restoration Zeús preserves the acute accent and long diphthong; the macron-only form Zeus is an accepted fallback. The domain encodes to Punycode while displaying the Greek-accented Latin form.

sources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

steps: The name is written rꜥ (𓂋𓂝) with the sun-disk (𓇳) as a determinative/rebus for 'sun'.
The consonantal skeleton r-ꜥ is vocalised as Ra in Egyptological convention; the original vocalisation is unknown.
Coptic ⲣⲏ provides a late phonetic reflex.
From the New Kingdom onward Ra is frequently combined with Amun as Amun-Ra.
provenance.etymology: Probably identical with Egyptian rꜥ 'sun, day'; the sun-god as the visible solar disk.
provenance.semantics: Sun-god, creator, and king of the gods; central deity of the Heliopolitan cosmogony.

variants.context: Syncretised form from the New Kingdom

uncertainties: The original vocalisation is not recorded; 'Ra' is a modern convention.
The role of the ꜥ (ayin) consonant is disputed; some readings treat the name as rꜥ with the sun determinative.
provenance.dnsNotes: The Unicode form Rꜥ uses the Egyptological alef/ayin characters (U+A722/U+A725), registrable in .com as Punycode; the hieroglyphic form is not used because hieroglyphs are outside the .com IDN table.

sources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

signs.name: þurs
signs.note: Voiceless dental fricative; in later manuscripts written <þ>.

signs.name: úr
signs.note: In this name the rune likely denotes a long rounded back vowel /uː/ or /oː/.

signs.name: reið
signs.note: Simple /r/; the geminate -rr- of normalized Þórr is not shown in runic spelling.

steps: The Viking-Age runic form ᚦᚢᚱ (þur) is attested on artefacts such as the Mannegårde coin graffiti.
The normalized Old Norse name is Þórr, with long /oː/ and geminate /rː/.
The name continues Proto-Germanic *Þunraz ('thunder'), with loss of the medial nasal and contraction.
Younger Futhark does not distinguish short/long vowels or voiced/voiceless stops, so ᚦᚢᚱ is a minimal phonetic skeleton.
provenance.etymology: From Proto-Germanic *Þunraz, 'thunder'. Cognates: Old English Þunor, Old High German Donar, Continental Germanic *Thunaraz.
provenance.semantics: God of thunder, lightning, storms, oak trees, and the protection of mankind.
uncertainties: The vowel quality of the runic spelling is ambiguous; ᚢ may represent /uː/, /oː/, or /øː/.
The Proto-Germanic reconstruction *Þunraz is widely accepted but the exact North-Germanic phonetic development is debated.
provenance.dnsNotes: The Unicode restoration Þórr uses Thorn (Þ) and acute-accented o, both registrable in .com. The runic form is not used as the primary domain because runic TLD support and keyboard input are impractical.

sources.title: Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

signs.name: śa + i vowel sign
signs.note: Devanagari śa (श) with the short i vowel sign (ि) gives śi.

signs.name: va
signs.note: Devanagari va with inherent short a; the final vowel is reduced (schwa deletion) in Sanskrit pronunciation.

steps: Sanskrit Śiva is written शिव in Devanagari.
The aksaras are शि (śi) and व (va); the inherent /a/ of व is phonetically reduced in connected speech.
The name means 'the auspicious one', an epithet that rises from Vedic Rudra to become one of the supreme deities of Hinduism.
IAST Ś retains the haček convention; Devanagari श is a palatal sibilant.
provenance.etymology: From Sanskrit śiva- 'auspicious, gracious, benevolent'. Related to the Vedic Rudra-Śiva complex.
provenance.semantics: Supreme deity (Trimurti as destroyer/regenerator), ascetic, lord of yoga, and cosmic dancer.
uncertainties: The original Vedic accent and precise morphological history of Śiva as a theonym are debated.
The relationship between Vedic Rudra and later Śiva involves a long syncretic development.
provenance.dnsNotes: The IAST form Śiva uses the acute on S (U+015A) and macron on i, registrable in .com. The Devanagari form is not used as a domain because Indic scripts are not supported in the .com IDN table.

signs.name: lóng 'dragon'
signs.note: The character depicts a stylised dragon; simplified form 龙.

steps: The Chinese character 龍 (simplified 龙) represents the dragon, a central cosmological creature in Chinese religion and imperial symbolism.
Modern Mandarin reading is lóng (second tone), written in Pinyin with an acute accent.
Old Chinese reconstructions include *C-rjoŋ or *mə-roŋ (Baxter-Sagart); the initial consonant cluster is debated.
The Unicode restoration Lóng preserves the Mandarin tone mark; the ASCII form loses tone and therefore meaning-distinctive information.
provenance.etymology: The character is both pictographic and phono-semantic; its phonetic component has been linked to words for 'dragon' across Sino-Tibetan.
provenance.semantics: Dragon, symbol of imperial power, rain, fertility, and yang energy.
uncertainties: Old Chinese reconstruction of the initial is debated (*C-rjoŋ vs. *mə-roŋ).
The exact morphological relationship to other Sino-Tibetan 'dragon' words remains uncertain.
provenance.dnsNotes: Pinyin Lóng with acute is registrable; the tone mark is the single distinctive feature preserved in the Unicode restoration.

signs.name: nichi / hi / hi 'sun'
signs.note: Kanji for 'sun' / 'day'; read nichi in on'yomi, hi in kun'yomi.

signs.name: kō / hikari 'light'
signs.note: Kanji for 'light'; the on'yomi kō supplies the long -ō of Nikkō.

steps: 日光 is a Sino-Japanese compound: 日 'sun' + 光 'light', hence 'sunlight'.
The standard Hepburn romanisation is Nikkō, with a macron over the final o marking a long vowel.
The geminate consonant -kk- reflects the sequential voicing assimilation of 日 (nichi) + 光 (kō) → Nikkō.
The place name Nikkō is famous for the Tōshō-gū shrine, dedicated to Tokugawa Ieyasu.
provenance.etymology: From Middle Chinese *nyit-kwang 'sunlight' (日 *nyit + 光 *kwang); borrowed into Japanese as Sino-Japanese nikkō.
provenance.semantics: Sunlight; by extension the sacred site and UNESCO World Heritage complex at Nikkō.
uncertainties: The exact historical accent and pitch pattern of the place name have varied by dialect and period.
The semantic narrowing from generic 'sunlight' to the place name is historical, not etymological.
provenance.dnsNotes: Nikkō with macron is Tier 1 because the long vowel is the only distinctive feature; the ASCII form Nikko loses length. The kanji form is not used as a .com domain because Japanese scripts are not in the .com IDN table.

signs.name: dalet (dagesh forte)
signs.note: With dagesh, the stop /d/; without it, the fricative /ð/ in Biblical Hebrew.

signs.name: qāmeṣ
signs.note: Long back vowel /ɔː/ or /aː/ in Tiberian pointing.

signs.name: vav
signs.note: Here functions as a mater for the long /ô/ vowel and as part of the diphthong /aw/.

signs.name: ḥīreq
signs.note: Short or long /i/ vowel.

signs.name: dalet
signs.note: Final letter; the lack of dagesh indicates spirantisation in post-vocalic position.

steps: The Masoretic spelling דָּוִד (Dāwîḏ) is preserved in the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia.
The first dalet carries a dagesh (דּ) because it follows a silent shewa at the beginning of the word, marking the stop /d/.
The vav (ו) with qāmeṣ and ḥīreq points indicates the diphthongal sequence /awī/.
The name is traditionally explained as from the root d-w-d 'beloved', though some scholars connect it to a Northwest Semitic theophoric element.
provenance.etymology: Popularly derived from Hebrew d-w-d 'to love', hence 'beloved'. Alternative proposals link it to a divine name or to a Hurrian/Northeast Semitic element.
provenance.semantics: Second king of Israel, unifier of the tribes, reputed psalmist, and ancestor in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions.
uncertainties: Etymology from d-w-d 'beloved' is traditional but not universally accepted; a theophoric origin has been proposed.
The exact Tiberian vowel quality of qāmeṣ is debated (/ɔː/ vs. /aː/).
provenance.dnsNotes: The academic transliteration Dāwîḏ uses macron and circumflex characters registrable in .com; the Hebrew form with vowel points is not used as the domain because combining marks complicate IDN registration.
